title: URL Generation
description: Learn how to generate URLs dynamically from route names and action names instead of hardcoding paths. Covers Url.Action, Url.RouteUrl, Html.ActionLink, and the IUrlHelper interface.

blocks.text: **URL generation** is the practice of creating URLs dynamically based on your application's routing configuration, rather than hardcoding paths in your views and controllers. When you change a route pattern later, every dynamically generated URL updates automatically — hardcoded paths do not.

ASP.NET Core provides several helpers for URL generation, each suited to different contexts: `Url.Action` for controllers, `Url.RouteUrl` for named routes, `Html.ActionLink` for generating complete anchor tags, and `IUrlHelper` for advanced scenarios.
Why Not Hardcode URLs?

Hardcoding a URL like `<a href="/Products/Details/5">` seems harmless at first. But consider what happens when you later change the route pattern to `/shop/product/5` or add a localization prefix like `/en/products/5`. Every hardcoded link in every view breaks silently.

blocks.title: Hardcoded URLs are a maintenance trap
blocks.text: Even a small routing change can break dozens of hardcoded links across many views. Dynamic URL generation ensures your links always reflect the current routing configuration, eliminating a whole category of bugs.
Url.Action: Generate URLs by Controller and Action
`Url.Action` generates a URL by specifying the action name, controller name, and route values. It looks up the matching route and returns the correct URL string.

blocks.title: Using Url.Action in a Razor view
blocks.content: Generate a URL to the Details action in the Products controller with a route value for the id.
blocks.code: @* Generates /Products/Details/5 *@ View Product 5 @* Generates /Products (default action) *@ All Products @* Generates / (home page) *@ Home

blocks.text: `Url.Action` returns the full path (e.g., `/Products/Details/5`). If your application is hosted in a virtual directory (e.g., `https://example.com/myapp/`), it automatically includes the application path.
Url.RouteUrl: Generate URLs by Route Name

When you name your routes using the `name` parameter in `MapControllerRoute`, you can generate URLs by route name using `Url.RouteUrl`. This is the most resilient approach because it does not depend on controller or action names.

blocks.title: Named routes and Url.RouteUrl
blocks.content: Name your routes in Program.cs and generate URLs by route name.

blocks.title: Name important routes
blocks.text: Naming your routes makes URL generation more resilient and your code more readable. `Url.RouteUrl("product-details", ...)` is self-documenting compared to `Url.Action("Details", "Products", ...)` which requires you to know the controller name.
Html.ActionLink: Generate Complete Anchor Tags
`Html.ActionLink` is a convenience helper that generates a complete `` tag with the correct `href` attribute. It is equivalent to writing `...` but in a single method call.

blocks.title: Using Html.ActionLink
blocks.content: Generate complete anchor tags with Html.ActionLink for links to other actions.

blocks.text: Generating URLs in Controllers
The same `Url` helper is available in controllers via the `ControllerBase.Url` property. This is useful when you need to redirect to a specific URL or build absolute URLs for emails or notifications.

blocks.title: URL generation in a controller action
blocks.content: Generate URLs inside a controller for redirects, emails, or API responses.

blocks.text: Note the `protocol: Request.Scheme` parameter. Without it, `Url.Action` returns a relative path (e.g., `/Products/Details/5`). With it, you get an absolute URL (e.g., `https://localhost:5001/Products/Details/5`) suitable for emails and external links.
The IUrlHelper Interface

`Url` in controllers and views is an instance of `IUrlHelper`. If you need URL generation outside of controllers or views (e.g., in a service class), you can inject `IUrlHelperFactory` and `IActionContextAccessor` to create your own `IUrlHelper` instance.

blocks.title: IUrlHelper in services
blocks.text: Generating URLs in service classes requires `IUrlHelperFactory` and `IActionContextAccessor`. This is an advanced scenario — most URL generation should happen in controllers or views where `Url` is already available.
Current Request URL Helpers
Sometimes you need parts of the current request URL — the path, query string, or host. ASP.NET Core provides access to these through the `HttpRequest` object.

blocks.title: Accessing current request URL parts
blocks.content: Use the HttpContext to read the current request's path, query string, and host.

terms.definition: Generates a URL from a controller action name and route values. Returns a relative URL path.
Generates a URL from a named route and route values. More resilient than Url.Action because it does not depend on controller or action names.
Generates a complete HTML anchor tag (<a>) with the correct href attribute based on an action, controller, and route values.
The interface behind the Url helper in controllers and views. Provides methods for generating URLs and links within your application.
A full URL including the protocol and host (e.g., https://example.com/Products/5). Generated by passing protocol: Request.Scheme to Url.Action.

blocks.title: URL generation methods at a glance
items: **Url.Action** — generates a URL from a controller action name and route values
**Url.RouteUrl** — generates a URL from a named route — the most resilient approach
**Html.ActionLink** — generates a complete anchor tag with the correct href attribute
**IUrlHelper** — the interface behind the Url helper, usable outside controllers and views

blocks.title: Replace Hardcoded Links with Dynamic URLs
blocks.description: Find and replace hardcoded URL links in a view with Url.Action and Url.RouteUrl calls.
steps: Create a layout view with a navigation bar containing links: Home, Products, About, Contact
Replace hardcoded href values like `/` and `/Products` with `@Url.Action("Index", "Home")` and `@Url.Action("Index", "Products")`
Add a named route in Program.cs: `app.MapControllerRoute("about", "About", new { controller = "Home", action = "About" })`
In the Products Index view, add links to Details pages using `@Url.Action("Details", "Products", new { id = product.Id })`
Change the default route pattern in Program.cs to `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}/info`
Confirm all dynamically generated links still work correctly (hardcoded links would now be broken)
blocks.expectedOutcome: All navigation links use dynamic URL generation. After changing the route pattern, only the hardcoded links (if any remain) break — all Url.Action and Url.RouteUrl links continue to work correctly.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Url.Action generates URLs from controller/action names and route values
Url.RouteUrl generates URLs from named routes — the most resilient approach
Html.ActionLink creates a complete anchor tag with the correct href in one call
IUrlHelper is the interface behind the Url helper, available in controllers and views
Pass protocol: Request.Scheme to generate absolute URLs for emails and external use
Named routes make your application more maintainable when URL patterns change
blocks.takeaway: Dynamic URL generation is a best practice that prevents a whole class of bugs when your routing configuration changes. Use Url.Action, Url.RouteUrl, or Html.ActionLink everywhere instead of hardcoding paths.
